extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and administrators applying for or managing NIH grants (K, F, R, SBIR/STTR, MIRA, etc.)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, mechanism-specific advice and procedural standards for preparing, submitting, tracking, and responding to NIH grant applications (A0/A1, K, R01, R21, R56, R36, STTR/SBIR, MIRA), and for interacting with Program Officials and Grants Management Specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: No duplicate or highly overlapping applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH will not accept duplicate or highly overlapping applications under review at the same time. An individual may not have two or more competing NIH career development applications pending review concurrently. In addition, NIH will not accept: An application that has substantial overlap with another application pending appeal of initial peer review (see NOT-OD-11-101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit essentially the same science to multiple NIH calls at the same time. Discuss plans with Program Officials, particularly for career development awards (K series), which are explicitly prohibited from being concurrent. If you have two truly independent projects, consider a different activity code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers judge the current application on its own (prior materials generally not seen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers don’t see any prior summary statements except for A1s, and they don’t see prior proposals. Reviewers must destroy all materials after the study section meeting, and even if a reviewer who was on the panel when your last application was reviewed remembers your proposal, they must judge the scientific merit of the current application on its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume prior awards (e.g., R56) bias reviewers in favor of a new A0. Prepare the current application to stand alone; integrate any progress from prior funding into the current page limits rather than relying on reviewers' memory of previous submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: A1/R56 renewal and project-year counting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The A1 R56 is not renewable; a new A0 should be the continuation of the R56 project. If a fundable score is achieved on the new A0 (or its A1), the new award will be for 4 years and not 5 because the R56 is considered as Year 1 of the new grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan resubmissions accordingly (expect shorter remaining project period if funded) and consult the PO about timelines; a gap between R56 end and new R01 start is allowed and does not affect funding likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress reports not allowed in A0; Introduction page use limited to A1
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot include a progress report. The ASSIST application will not allow this for anything but a Type 2 application. You can’t try to add it as another attachment. The Introduction page is for A1s (resubmissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting R56 results into a new A0, integrate progress and new data into the regular page-limited sections (e.g., within the 12-page Research Strategy) rather than attempting to attach a separate progress report or an Introduction reserved for A1s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of Just-in-Time (JIT) requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Often but not always (an official JIT) results in funding. At the end of the FY, decisions are made based on both programmatic priority and which awards can be made quickly (no regulatory approval needed, simple administrative review). Whether you receive an award depends on how much $ is left by the time your application gets to the top of the list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A JIT request signals potential movement toward award but is not a guarantee. Prepare required JIT materials promptly when requested; having JIT information ready can speed award processing at year-end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status pages update asynchronously
rubrics_metrics.description: There were many times that updates were populated first on the status information page, and days later on the status results page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect delays and staggered status updates in eRA Commons; do not over-interpret a single status change and allow for lag between different tracking pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subaward administration goes through the prime grantee; NoA shows subaward amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The subaward goes through the prime grantee. All NoAs show the subaward amounts. The subaward details will be on the PI’s NoA, because the PI is responsible for that work being done and progress being reported as part of the annual RPPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subawardees typically will not get separate NOAs from NIH; the prime institution issues subcontracts. If subaward issuance is delayed, check with your grants management specialist for missing regulatory approvals (IACUC/IRB) or other documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative supplement processing and eRA visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the GMS requested clarification, then they are processing your application; whether you receive the supplement will likely depend on whether the IACUC and budget information is acceptable. The awards are made internally, so you probably won’t see your eRA status change if/until an award is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For admin supplement status, rely on PO and GMS communications rather than expecting eRA Commons to show intermediate processing steps; ask the PO if you need to know whether the application is on a paylist.

rubrics_metrics.name: IC paylines and appropriations determine funding likelihood; interim paylines conservative
rubrics_metrics.description: ICs are very conservative at the outset of an FY if they don’t have their appropriation yet. If ICs post interim paylines, they can raise them later and go back and pick up additional awards from earlier cycles that were within the later, higher payline. Funding depends on appropriations, programmatic priorities, and number of applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume posted interim paylines are final; expect possible increases later in the year. Budgetary uncertainty (e.g., delayed appropriations, supplemental funding, COVID-related changes) affects paylines and award decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project period vs budget period timing and carryover
rubrics_metrics.description: The budget period starts when the award is made, and next year, the budget and project periods should match. If you had funds carried over from the prior project period, your competitive renewal will be reduced by this amount for the first year (and you’ll have been able to keep working).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A shorter first budget year does not necessarily mean lost funds or lost time: carryover funds and subsequent carryover policies can affect actual usable time. Check NoA details and discuss with grants admin if dates look problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission strategy: A0 vs A1 and study section selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application was not discussed, often it is better simply to submit a new A0, since there was no prior discussion to address (the main point of the Introduction for A1s). You should change study sections if there is one better suited to review your application – not just to avoid the prior reviewers. Contact a PO about aims and study section recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between A0 and A1 based on whether you have discrete critiques to address; use ART and Matchmaker to identify appropriate study sections; POs can advise on resubmission strategy and suitable SRGs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers evaluate each application on scientific merit; overlapping methods acceptable if aims distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are instructed to review each application on the basis of its scientific merit. It is up to the ICs, not the SRGs, to decide if they want to fund two applications for the same PI in the same cycle. As long as the aims and objectives are distinct, an overlapping methodology applied to two different projects should be fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If submitting multiple applications in the same cycle, ensure aims/aims' scope are distinct and justify independence; consult the PO(s) if in doubt about perceived overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent effort vs salary are separate budgeting concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent effort and salary drawn are 2 separate things. You can’t take more salary than your effort but you can take less. Unless, like some Med Schools, they force you to take salary that = your effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you change percent effort (e.g., reduce from 100% to 85%), expect salary adjustments accordingly, but the overall non-salary budget typically remains unchanged. Coordinate with institutional HR/grants offices for NOA amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-cost-extension and Type 3 revision carryover: check the NoA
rubrics_metrics.description: The NoA for your Type 3 revision award (distinct from the parent award) states whether you have automatic carryover or if prior approval is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume automatic extension or carryover; verify terms in the Notice of Award and confirm with your grants administrator or GMS if unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'deferral' in funding notices
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice stating a decision to fund your application has been deferred by an IC likely means deferring a decision until the next fiscal year; sometimes deferral gives time to submit an amended application next year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact your PO to clarify the reason for deferral and whether relinquishing to a secondary IC is advisable. Deferral is not an outright denial and may be routine administrative timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: IC-specific procedures like MIRA acceptance requests
rubrics_metrics.description: For MIRA awards, NIGMS may ask you to send an email stating that you will accept the MIRA award; this request indicates that NIGMS intends to fund your application (assuming subsequent administrative review does not uncover problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some ICs request explicit acceptance prior to full administrative processing to avoid wasting administrative effort on applicants who will decline; respond promptly when asked to confirm intent to accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect delays during systemic disruptions (e.g., COVID-19) and when FY ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything – at every IC – is taking longer due to COVID-19, plus they are busy with the end of the FY scramble. This is the season of hurry up and wait. Application processing will happen quickly when it does, so if you need regulatory approvals for JIT, you might look into that in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be patient and avoid repeatedly contacting PO/GMS in the short term; if status remains pending after a reasonable extra interval (e.g., several weeks beyond expected), then check with GMS for needed documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing JIT and regulatory approvals in advance speeds award processing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have your JIT ready, you can go ahead and submit it online so it’s there, or you can wait until they ask for it – they won’t request it until they are sure your application will move forward for funding. You will only have a day or two to submit JIT if the request comes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have IACUC/IRB and other regulatory documentation, budget clarifications, and data sharing plans prepared so that an official JIT can be completed quickly when requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory approvals (IACUC/IRB) can delay subawards and award preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: You can contact the GMS to see if there was an administrative hold-up on issuing the subcontract award (i.e., missing IACUC or IRB approval or other required documentation). If so, the subaward will be made when any required documentation is in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure institutional compliance approvals are completed and communicated to GMS early to avoid administrative delays in subaward issuance or NOA finalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct roles of Program Official (PO) and Grants Management Specialist (GMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer any questions to Program Official or Grants Management Specialist. POs recommend and advise on science, study sections, and programmatic interest; GMS handles award processing and administrative reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate with your PO for scientific/resubmission strategy and with your GMS for administrative, budgetary, and award-status questions. POs are not involved in the final award processing steps.
